summary:
Northern Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, and no law of the region displaces it. National provisions on legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination and marriage recognition apply here as they do elsewhere in the country; the national assessment is carried in full by the Philippines record.

Protection at the sub-national level is thin. Reporting cited in the national rights overview records that by mid-2019 only four local government units across the whole of Mindanao had passed pro-LGBT ordinances. Northern Mindanao is one of the regions within Mindanao, and the inventory lists no ordinance of its own for any of its provinces or cities.

Lanao del Norte, within the region, has Muslim personal-law courts in operation alongside the ordinary courts. The sources record no ruling, practice note or case from those courts involving a trans applicant or a trans person's marriage.

No trans-specific killing, assault, prosecution or enforcement action in Northern Mindanao appears in the source inventory. The trans-specific violence the sources describe is recorded in other parts of the country and is carried by the national record; nothing in the inventory places such an incident in this region.
tangentialFactors:
The only regional-scale figure in the inventory is the mid-2019 count of four pro-LGBT ordinances across Mindanao. No later count for the island group or for Northern Mindanao appears in the sources, so the current number of local government units in the region offering that coverage is not established.

The trans-specific violence documented in the sources lies outside this region, and the national legislative campaign it prompted does not itself generate obligations at regional or local level. Nothing in the inventory ties a trans-specific incident, prosecution or official statement to Northern Mindanao.
localsOnly:
Residents in Northern Mindanao depend on ordinances passed by their own local government units for anti-discrimination protection. The inventory lists no ordinance passed by a local government unit in the region, and the mid-2019 Mindanao count of four such ordinances indicates how few units across the island group had extended that coverage at the time.

Muslim personal-law courts operate in Lanao del Norte, within the region, so personal-status matters for Muslim residents there may be adjudicated in that channel. The sources do not record how a trans resident's marriage, name or gender marker would be handled in it, and that point is unresolved.
outOfScopeNotes:
Documentation for Northern Mindanao is sparse, and the absence of a regional signal does not establish that no divergence from the national picture exists. No Northern Mindanao ordinance text, court ruling, detention practice or enforcement record is sourced here, so the region's practical treatment of trans visitors and residents is not independently verified.

The inventory gives no region-specific detail on policing, custodial placement, health care, facilities access or partner recognition in Northern Mindanao. Those matters are not sourced for this region and are not asserted either way.
